title: GitHub Actions for Free 24/7 AI Automation
summary:
The Problem With Cloud AI

Every token costs money. Every API call adds up. And your data goes to their servers.

The Local Alternative 

brew install ollama
ollama pull llama3.2
ollama serve

Now you have a GPT-4 level model running on your MacBook. Free. Private. Fast.

Real Code Example 

import requests

def ask_local_ai(question):
    r = requests.post(
        "http://localhost:11434/api/generate",
        json={"model": "llama3.2", "prompt": question, "stream": False}
    )
    return r.json()["response"]

# Works immediately, no API key needed
answer = ask_local_ai("Explain Docker in one paragraph")
print(answer)

title: Zero Trust Between Services, Not Just Users: A Practical Pattern for Multi-Cloud Estates
summary:
Most zero-trust conversations start with people: single sign-on, MFA, device posture, and conditional access for engineers and employees. That work matters. It is also only half the traffic in a modern estate.

The other half never touches a browser. A checkout service calls an inventory service. A reporting job reads from a database in another cloud. An inference endpoint receives requests from an application running somewhere else entirely. Those service-to-service calls are usually trusted because of where they come from — a VPC, a subnet, a VPN tunnel, a private range that was considered safe when it was drawn.

That assumption is the problem zero trust was meant to remove. If network location is the credential, then anything that reaches that network segment inherits the trust, including a compromised workload, a misconfigured job, and a test service that was never meant to run in production.

1. Give every workload an identity that is not an IP address

The first step is separating identity from location.

A workload identity should answer three questions on every call: which service is calling, in which environment, and with what proof that the identity was issued recently to that exact workload?

Patterns that hold up in practice:

  • Short-lived credentials over static keys. A token or certificate that expires in minutes limits the damage from a leak in a way a long-lived API key copied into configuration never can. Rotation stops being a calendar event when issuance is automatic.
  • Identity bound to the workload, not the host. Containers move, instances are replaced, and jobs run once and disappear. Tying trust to a machine name or an address breaks in exactly the environments where automation is working correctly.
  • Separate identities per environment. Production, staging, and development should not share a service identity, even when they share code. Environment confusion is a common incident pattern; distinct identities make it a policy denial instead of a data incident.
  • No shared service accounts across teams. When five services authenticate as the same generic account, logs can show what happened but not who did it. Per-service identity is what makes an authorization policy, and an audit trail, meaningful.

Cloud platforms across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle all offer workload identity mechanisms, but they do not automatically compose across clouds. In a multi-cloud estate, the design work is choosing one consistent identity model for cross-cloud calls instead of letting each cloud's defaults create a different trust story at every boundary.

2. Authorize the call, not just the connection

A firewall rule that allows one subnet to reach another on a port answers a connectivity question. It does not answer an authorization question.

Zero trust between services means each call is evaluated against policy: is this caller allowed to perform this action on this resource, in this environment, right now?

That evaluation does not need to be slow or centralised for every request, but it does need to be explicit:

  • Default deny between services. A new service should reach nothing until its outbound and inbound relationships are declared. The declaration is documentation that enforces itself.
  • Policy at the resource, not only at the perimeter. If a database accepts connections from the whole application tier, the tier is the perimeter. Narrow the rule to the named services that actually read and write that store.
  • Distinguish read, write, and admin paths. Many flat designs grant a reporting job the same path as the transactional service that owns the data. Separate policies for read-only consumers make least privilege practical instead of theoretical.
  • Make policy reviewable as code. A policy expressed in versioned configuration can be reviewed in a pull request, tested in staging, and rolled back. A policy that lives only as portal clicks cannot.

A useful test is to pick an internal service at random and ask: which named services are allowed to call it, and where is that written down in a form that would still be true after the team changes? If the answer is a diagram from last year, the policy does not really exist yet.

3. Encrypt and authenticate in transit, even on private paths

Private connectivity reduces exposure. It does not remove the need to authenticate the ends of a conversation.

Mutual TLS, signed tokens, or an equivalent authenticated transport should be the normal path for service-to-service traffic, including traffic that never leaves a private network. That provides two things a private route alone cannot: proof that the other end is the intended service, and protection if a route, tunnel, or segment is misconfigured later.

The operational lesson from teams that have rolled this out is to automate certificate and credential issuance from the start. Manual certificate handling is where service identity projects stall — not because the cryptography is hard, but because expiry becomes an outage pattern. Issuance, renewal, and revocation belong in the platform, with alerts on failed renewal long before expiry.

Start with the highest-value paths if a full rollout is unrealistic: calls that carry customer data, calls that cross a cloud or account boundary, and administrative interfaces. Then expand. A partial rollout with clear coverage is better than a mandate that every team quietly routes around.

4. Log the decision, not just the traffic

Traditional flow logs show that bytes moved between addresses. Zero-trust systems should also record the identity decision: which workload identity called which service, whether policy allowed it, and which policy version was in effect.

That record changes troubleshooting as much as it changes security:

  • A denied call from a legitimate service usually means a missing policy after a deployment, visible immediately instead of discovered as a silent failure.
  • An allowed call from an unexpected identity is a signal worth alerting on, even if the data accessed was ordinary.
  • Repeated denials from the same workload often reveal a stale configuration or a retired service that was never decommissioned.

Treat denials as telemetry, review them weekly during a rollout, and tune policy from evidence. A zero-trust deployment that generates denials nobody reads trains teams to request broad permissions to make the noise stop — which recreates the flat network, one exception at a time.

5. Roll it out without rebuilding everything at once

The estates that succeed rarely start with a flag day. They start with inventory and observation:

  1. List the real service-to-service flows from flow logs and application dependencies, not from architecture diagrams alone.
  2. Issue identities to workloads in observe mode, logging which identity would have called what, before enforcing denial.
  3. Enforce default-deny first on new services, where there is no legacy behaviour to break.
  4. Move the highest-risk existing paths — cross-cloud, cross-environment, and data-store access — to authenticated, policy-checked calls.
  5. Retire the broad network rules those paths relied on. This last step is the actual security gain, and it is the step most often skipped, leaving the new controls layered on top of the old trust instead of replacing it.

That sequencing also clarifies where help is useful. Designing identity, policy, and private connectivity consistently across several clouds is the combined problem CloudVerg works on for US businesses — private cloud and AI connectivity with VergShield covering zero-trust security alongside the wider platform set (VergMesh, VergForge, VergMind, and VergRail): https://cloudverg.com

Whether the work is handled internally or with outside support, the measure of success is the same: a network location on its own should no longer be enough for one service to reach another.

A short checklist

For each important service-to-service path:

  • [ ] Caller and callee each have a distinct workload identity, separate per environment
  • [ ] Credentials are short-lived and issued automatically; no shared static keys remain on the path
  • [ ] Policy names which services may call which resources, with read, write, and admin separated
  • [ ] Default is deny; new services start with no access until relationships are declared
  • [ ] Transport is authenticated and encrypted, including on private routes
  • [ ] Allowed and denied calls are logged with identity and policy outcome, and denials are reviewed
  • [ ] Broad subnet-to-subnet rules retired once identity-based policy is enforced

Zero trust for users changed how people sign in. Zero trust between services changes something more fundamental: it replaces inherited trust in a network diagram with explicit, checkable permission for every conversation that matters. In a multi-cloud estate, that is the difference between a segmentation story and segmentation that actually holds.

title: Spring Boot: migrations at startup, health checks and metrics
summary:
Migrations are written in development, but they have to run wherever the application runs: on a colleague's laptop, in CI, in staging, in production. The simplest way to get there is to let the application apply them itself, each time it starts, before anything else touches the database.

This article adds the Migrax starter to a Spring Boot application, follows what happens at startup, starts two instances at once, and looks at what Actuator shows: a health check and Prometheus metrics. At the end, the pipeline runs the migrations instead of the application.

Tested with: Migrax 0.17.1, Spring Boot 3.5.7, Hibernate 6.6.33, Micrometer 1.15.5, PostgreSQL 17. Every output below was copied from a real run; log lines are shortened to the message.

The setup

A shop with two entities, Customer and PurchaseOrder. Besides the usual web and JPA starters, the application has Actuator, the Prometheus registry and the Migrax starter:


  org.springframework.boot
  spring-boot-starter-actuator


  io.micrometer
  micrometer-registry-prometheus


  org.migrax
  migrax-spring-boot-starter
  0.17.1

application.properties has the database, Hibernate set to only check the schema, and the two Actuator endpoints used below:

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,prometheus
management.endpoint.health.show-details=always

The migrations come from the entities. migrax init sets up the project (it reads the database settings from application.properties), and generate writes the first migration:

$ migrax generate
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customers
  - create table purchase_orders
  - add foreign key fk_purchase_orders_cu_1ba47d9c on purchase_orders
Rollback script written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.

The file sits in src/main/resources/db/migration, so it is packaged into the jar. That is where the starter looks.

What happens at startup

Start the application on the empty database:

HikariPool-1 - Start completed.
Migrax: Applying migration '0001_initial.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0001_initial.sql'.
Migrax: applied 1 migration(s)
Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'
Started ShopApplication in 9.05 seconds (process running for 10.302)

The order matters. The starter runs as soon as the connection pool is there and before JPA starts, so when Hibernate validates the schema, the tables already exist. With ddl-auto=validate, a database that doesn't match the entities stops the start, instead of failing on the first request.

Start it again and there is nothing to do:

Migrax: schema is up to date
Started ShopApplication in 8.571 seconds (process running for 9.58)

The application never needs the migrax command. It reads the migration files from the jar and records each one in the history table in the database, with a checksum.

Several instances starting together

A new field on Customer:

@Column(nullable = false, length = 2)
@ColumnDefault("'GB'")
private String country = "GB";

migrax generate writes 0002_add_customers_country.sql:

ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN country varchar(2) DEFAULT 'GB' NOT NULL;

In production, the new version rarely starts alone: two or more instances start at the same moment. Only one of them may apply the migration. Migrax takes a lock in the database first (on PostgreSQL an advisory lock), and by default an instance that doesn't get it stops at once. Here are the two instances, started together:

--- instance 1
Migrax: Applying migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'.
Migrax: applied 1 migration(s)
Started ShopApplication in 10.515 seconds (process running for 11.809)

--- instance 2
Caused by: org.migrax.dialect.MigrationLockHeldException: Another Migrax process is applying migrations.

Nothing is broken: the migration ran once. But the second instance failed and has to be restarted, and an orchestrator counts that as a crash. Tell the instances to wait for each other instead:

migrax.lock-timeout=2m

To make the wait visible, the next run has more to do. The table now has two million customers, and an index on full_name is added to the entity (@Table(indexes = @Index(columnList = "fullName"))). generate writes it as 0003_index_customers.sql, and warns about it:

src/main/resources/db/migration/0003_index_customers.sql, statement 1: warning MX001
  CREATE INDEX idx_customers_full_name ON customers (full_name)
  Building this index blocks writes to customers until it finishes.
  Fix: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own migration that starts with '-- migrax:no-transaction' ('migrax generate --safe' does this).

Worth knowing on a busy table. Here it is fine. Both instances start again, with 0002 and 0003 pending (0002 was rolled back to run again):

--- instance 1
Migrax: Applying migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'.
Migrax: Applying migration '0003_index_customers.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0003_index_customers.sql'.
Migrax: applied 2 migration(s)
Started ShopApplication in 17.185 seconds (process running for 18.461)

--- instance 2
Migrax: Another Migrax process holds the migration lock; waiting up to 2m...
Migrax: schema is up to date
Started ShopApplication in 18.851 seconds (process running for 20.138)

The second instance waited until the first had built the index, found nothing left to do, and started. Set the timeout longer than your slowest migration takes; when it runs out, the instance stops as before.

The health check

With Actuator in the application, the starter adds a migrax health component:

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/health/migrax
{"status":"UP","details":{"applied":3,"pending":0,"problems":0}}

problems counts migrations that failed, were edited after they were applied, or are in the history but no longer in the jar. Any of those, or a pending migration, makes the component DOWN. Turn it off with management.health.migrax.enabled=false.

An edited migration is the one people run into. Someone changes varchar(20) to varchar(30) in a migration that production has already applied, and the next start stops:

Caused by: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'migraxMigrator' defined in class path resource [org/migrax/spring/MigraxAutoConfiguration.class]: Checksum changed for applied migration 0004_add_purchase_orders_status.sql

The database already has the old version of that migration, and it never gets the new one. Leave applied migrations alone; a change goes into a new migration.

Metrics

The application has a Micrometer registry (here Prometheus), so Migrax records its migrations there without any setting. After the run above, the first instance shows:

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus | grep ^migrax
migrax_lock_wait_seconds_max{database="default"} 0.044737607
migrax_migration_seconds_max{database="default",migration="0002_add_customers_country.sql",outcome="success"} 0.005012614
migrax_migration_seconds_max{database="default",migration="0003_index_customers.sql",outcome="success"} 6.10576425
migrax_migrations_applied_total{database="default"} 2.0
migrax_migrations_pending{database="default"} 0.0
migrax_run_seconds_max{database="default",outcome="success"} 6.212559502

(Only the _max lines of each timer are shown; _count and _sum are there too.) The second instance, the one that waited:

migrax_lock_wait_seconds_max{database="default"} 7.803599713
migrax_run_seconds_max{database="default",outcome="success"} 7.843474718

That answers the questions that come up after a slow deployment: which migration took the time (the index, 6.1 seconds), and how long the other instances waited for it (7.8 seconds). For an alert, the counter of failed migrations is the one to watch:

- alert: MigraxMigrationFailed
  expr: increase(migrax_migrations_failed_total[15m]) > 0

With an OpenTelemetry bean, each run and each migration also becomes a span in the trace of the startup. migrax.metrics.enabled=false and migrax.tracing.enabled=false turn them off.

When a pipeline migrates

Some teams don't let the application change the schema. A deployment pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations, and the application only reads. One setting:

migrax.migrate-at-startup=false

The order then becomes the pipeline's job. A new status column on PurchaseOrder, deployed before the pipeline has migrated, doesn't get far:

Migrax: not migrating at startup (migrax.migrate-at-startup=false); 1 migration(s) pending
Caused by: org.hibernate.tool.schema.spi.SchemaManagementException: Schema-validation: missing column [status] in table [purchase_orders]

That is ddl-auto=validate doing its job. So: run migrax migrate (or the Maven goal migrax:migrate) as a step before the new version starts:

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0004_add_purchase_orders_status.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0004_add_purchase_orders_status.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 4 total in src/main/resources/db/migration.

Not every pending migration stops the start. An index isn't checked by Hibernate's validation, so a release with a forgotten index migration (0005) starts fine, and is slow. That is where the health check and the pending gauge come in, because they keep working when the application doesn't migrate:

$ curl -s -w ' HTTP %{http_code}\n' localhost:8080/actuator/health/migrax
{"status":"DOWN","details":{"applied":4,"pending":1,"problems":0}} HTTP 503

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus | grep ^migrax
migrax_migrations_pending{database="default"} 1.0

An alert on the gauge catches a pipeline step that was skipped:

- alert: MigraxMigrationsPending
  expr: migrax_migrations_pending > 0
  for: 30m

To keep traffic away from such an instance on Kubernetes, add the component to the readiness group:

management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readinessState,migrax

Once the pipeline has run migrax migrate, the application notices on its own. It asks the database at most every 10 seconds, so no restart is needed:

$ curl -s -w ' HTTP %{http_code}\n' localhost:8080/actuator/health/migrax
{"status":"UP","details":{"applied":5,"pending":0,"problems":0}} HTTP 200

Summary

  • Add migrax-spring-boot-starter, keep the migrations in src/main/resources/db/migration, and the application applies them each time it starts, before JPA, so ddl-auto=validate checks the migrated schema.
  • Several instances: set migrax.lock-timeout (for example 2m). One instance migrates, the others wait and then start.
  • With Actuator, the migrax health component is DOWN for a pending, failed, edited or missing migration. With Micrometer, metrics show how long each migration took and how long the instances waited.
  • When a pipeline migrates, set migrax.migrate-at-startup=false, run migrax migrate before the new version starts, and alert on migrax_migrations_pending.

More in the docs: Spring Boot, Metrics and tracing and Containers and Kubernetes.

Originally published at migrax.org.

application.properties has the database, Hibernate set to only check the schema, and the two Actuator endpoints used below:

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
spring.datasource.username=shop
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,prometheus
management.endpoint.health.show-details=always

The migrations come from the entities. migrax init sets up the project (it reads the database settings from application.properties), and generate writes the first migration:

$ migrax generate
No snapshot yet: using the current database schema as the baseline.
Created src/main/resources/db/migration/0001_initial.sql:
  - create table customers
  - create table purchase_orders
  - add foreign key fk_purchase_orders_cu_1ba47d9c on purchase_orders
Rollback script written to src/main/resources/db/migration/rollback.
Review the SQL, then run 'migrax migrate'.

The file sits in src/main/resources/db/migration, so it is packaged into the jar. That is where the starter looks.

What happens at startup

Start the application on the empty database:

HikariPool-1 - Start completed.
Migrax: Applying migration '0001_initial.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0001_initial.sql'.
Migrax: applied 1 migration(s)
Tomcat started on port 8080 (http) with context path '/'
Started ShopApplication in 9.05 seconds (process running for 10.302)

The order matters. The starter runs as soon as the connection pool is there and before JPA starts, so when Hibernate validates the schema, the tables already exist. With ddl-auto=validate, a database that doesn't match the entities stops the start, instead of failing on the first request.

Start it again and there is nothing to do:

Migrax: schema is up to date
Started ShopApplication in 8.571 seconds (process running for 9.58)

The application never needs the migrax command. It reads the migration files from the jar and records each one in the history table in the database, with a checksum.

Several instances starting together

A new field on Customer:

@Column(nullable = false, length = 2)
@ColumnDefault("'GB'")
private String country = "GB";

migrax generate writes 0002_add_customers_country.sql:

ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN country varchar(2) DEFAULT 'GB' NOT NULL;

In production, the new version rarely starts alone: two or more instances start at the same moment. Only one of them may apply the migration. Migrax takes a lock in the database first (on PostgreSQL an advisory lock), and by default an instance that doesn't get it stops at once. Here are the two instances, started together:

--- instance 1
Migrax: Applying migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'.
Migrax: applied 1 migration(s)
Started ShopApplication in 10.515 seconds (process running for 11.809)

--- instance 2
Caused by: org.migrax.dialect.MigrationLockHeldException: Another Migrax process is applying migrations.

Nothing is broken: the migration ran once. But the second instance failed and has to be restarted, and an orchestrator counts that as a crash. Tell the instances to wait for each other instead:

migrax.lock-timeout=2m

To make the wait visible, the next run has more to do. The table now has two million customers, and an index on full_name is added to the entity (@Table(indexes = @Index(columnList = "fullName"))). generate writes it as 0003_index_customers.sql, and warns about it:

src/main/resources/db/migration/0003_index_customers.sql, statement 1: warning MX001
  CREATE INDEX idx_customers_full_name ON customers (full_name)
  Building this index blocks writes to customers until it finishes.
  Fix: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own migration that starts with '-- migrax:no-transaction' ('migrax generate --safe' does this).

Worth knowing on a busy table. Here it is fine. Both instances start again, with 0002 and 0003 pending (0002 was rolled back to run again):

--- instance 1
Migrax: Applying migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0002_add_customers_country.sql'.
Migrax: Applying migration '0003_index_customers.sql'...
Migrax: Successfully applied migration '0003_index_customers.sql'.
Migrax: applied 2 migration(s)
Started ShopApplication in 17.185 seconds (process running for 18.461)

--- instance 2
Migrax: Another Migrax process holds the migration lock; waiting up to 2m...
Migrax: schema is up to date
Started ShopApplication in 18.851 seconds (process running for 20.138)

The second instance waited until the first had built the index, found nothing left to do, and started. Set the timeout longer than your slowest migration takes; when it runs out, the instance stops as before.

The health check

With Actuator in the application, the starter adds a migrax health component:

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/health/migrax
{"status":"UP","details":{"applied":3,"pending":0,"problems":0}}

problems counts migrations that failed, were edited after they were applied, or are in the history but no longer in the jar. Any of those, or a pending migration, makes the component DOWN. Turn it off with management.health.migrax.enabled=false.

An edited migration is the one people run into. Someone changes varchar(20) to varchar(30) in a migration that production has already applied, and the next start stops:

Caused by: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'migraxMigrator' defined in class path resource [org/migrax/spring/MigraxAutoConfiguration.class]: Checksum changed for applied migration 0004_add_purchase_orders_status.sql

The database already has the old version of that migration, and it never gets the new one. Leave applied migrations alone; a change goes into a new migration.

Metrics

The application has a Micrometer registry (here Prometheus), so Migrax records its migrations there without any setting. After the run above, the first instance shows:

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus | grep ^migrax
migrax_lock_wait_seconds_max{database="default"} 0.044737607
migrax_migration_seconds_max{database="default",migration="0002_add_customers_country.sql",outcome="success"} 0.005012614
migrax_migration_seconds_max{database="default",migration="0003_index_customers.sql",outcome="success"} 6.10576425
migrax_migrations_applied_total{database="default"} 2.0
migrax_migrations_pending{database="default"} 0.0
migrax_run_seconds_max{database="default",outcome="success"} 6.212559502

(Only the _max lines of each timer are shown; _count and _sum are there too.) The second instance, the one that waited:

migrax_lock_wait_seconds_max{database="default"} 7.803599713
migrax_run_seconds_max{database="default",outcome="success"} 7.843474718

That answers the questions that come up after a slow deployment: which migration took the time (the index, 6.1 seconds), and how long the other instances waited for it (7.8 seconds). For an alert, the counter of failed migrations is the one to watch:

- alert: MigraxMigrationFailed
  expr: increase(migrax_migrations_failed_total[15m]) > 0

With an OpenTelemetry bean, each run and each migration also becomes a span in the trace of the startup. migrax.metrics.enabled=false and migrax.tracing.enabled=false turn them off.

When a pipeline migrates

Some teams don't let the application change the schema. A deployment pipeline or a DBA runs the migrations, and the application only reads. One setting:

migrax.migrate-at-startup=false

The order then becomes the pipeline's job. A new status column on PurchaseOrder, deployed before the pipeline has migrated, doesn't get far:

Migrax: not migrating at startup (migrax.migrate-at-startup=false); 1 migration(s) pending
Caused by: org.hibernate.tool.schema.spi.SchemaManagementException: Schema-validation: missing column [status] in table [purchase_orders]

That is ddl-auto=validate doing its job. So: run migrax migrate (or the Maven goal migrax:migrate) as a step before the new version starts:

$ migrax migrate
Applying migration '0004_add_purchase_orders_status.sql'...
Successfully applied migration '0004_add_purchase_orders_status.sql'.
Applied 1 migration(s); 4 total in src/main/resources/db/migration.

Not every pending migration stops the start. An index isn't checked by Hibernate's validation, so a release with a forgotten index migration (0005) starts fine, and is slow. That is where the health check and the pending gauge come in, because they keep working when the application doesn't migrate:

$ curl -s -w ' HTTP %{http_code}\n' localhost:8080/actuator/health/migrax
{"status":"DOWN","details":{"applied":4,"pending":1,"problems":0}} HTTP 503

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus | grep ^migrax
migrax_migrations_pending{database="default"} 1.0

An alert on the gauge catches a pipeline step that was skipped:

- alert: MigraxMigrationsPending
  expr: migrax_migrations_pending > 0
  for: 30m

To keep traffic away from such an instance on Kubernetes, add the component to the readiness group:

management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=readinessState,migrax

Once the pipeline has run migrax migrate, the application notices on its own. It asks the database at most every 10 seconds, so no restart is needed:

$ curl -s -w ' HTTP %{http_code}\n' localhost:8080/actuator/health/migrax
{"status":"UP","details":{"applied":5,"pending":0,"problems":0}} HTTP 200

Summary

  • Add migrax-spring-boot-starter, keep the migrations in src/main/resources/db/migration, and the application applies them each time it starts, before JPA, so ddl-auto=validate checks the migrated schema.
  • Several instances: set migrax.lock-timeout (for example 2m). One instance migrates, the others wait and then start.
  • With Actuator, the migrax health component is DOWN for a pending, failed, edited or missing migration. With Micrometer, metrics show how long each migration took and how long the instances waited.
  • When a pipeline migrates, set migrax.migrate-at-startup=false, run migrax migrate before the new version starts, and alert on migrax_migrations_pending.

More in the docs: Spring Boot, Metrics and tracing and Containers and Kubernetes.

title: Docker Port Is Already Allocated: Fix Address Already in Use
summary:
You run docker run -p 8080:80 or docker compose up and Docker refuses to start the container. The message is either Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 failed: port is already allocated or Error starting userland proxy: listen tcp4 0.0.0.0:8080: bind: address already in use. The two look alike, but they point at different owners of the port, and the fix depends on which one you got.

This guide reproduces both errors with nginx:1.30.6-alpine on Docker Engine 26.1.5, then repeats them on Docker Engine 29.9.2 to show the newer wording. Every message below comes from that lab run on November 8, 2026. Demand for this fix is huge. On that day the Stack Overflow question Docker Error bind: address already in use had 1,095,795 views and Bind for 0.0.0.0:4000 failed: port is already allocated had 610,285.

The short version:

  • port is already allocated means another container already publishes that host port. Find it with docker ps --filter publish=8080, then stop it or change your host port.
  • bind: address already in use means something outside Docker's port table holds the port, usually a host service. Find it with sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :8080' and stop that service.
  • With Compose, the owner is often a project in another directory. Read its labels, then run docker compose -p NAME down.
  • A failed docker run leaves a container in the Created state. Remove it before you retry with the same name.
  • Stopping a container frees its port. Removing it is not required.

Table of contents

Fix port is already allocated

Start with the map. Match the message you see to the cause and the fix:

Reproduce it with two containers

The first container takes host port 8080. The second asks for the same host port:

docker run -d --name web1 -p 8080:80 nginx:1.30.6-alpine
docker run -d --name web2 -p 8080:80 nginx:1.30.6-alpine

The second command failed with exit code 125:

docker: Error response from daemon: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint web2 (494c5c95...): Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 failed: port is already allocated.

Docker tracks every published host port. When a running container already holds 0.0.0.0:8080, the daemon rejects the new mapping from its own records. The container port (80 in both cases) does not matter. Two containers can both listen on port 80 inside their own network namespaces. Only the host side collides. As the accepted Stack Overflow answer by yamenk puts it: "You need to make sure that the previous container you launched is killed, before launching a new one that uses the same port."

Find the container that owns the port

docker ps has a filter for published ports, so you don't have to scan the whole list:

docker ps --filter publish=8080 --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"

NAMES     STATUS         PORTS
web1      Up 5 seconds   0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp, :::8080->80/tcp

On the host, ss showed the listener as docker-proxy, one process for IPv4 and one for IPv6:

LISTEN 0      4096         0.0.0.0:8080      0.0.0.0:*    users:(("docker-proxy",pid=751939,fd=4))
LISTEN 0      4096            [::]:8080         [::]:*    users:(("docker-proxy",pid=751946,fd=4))

If you see docker-proxy there, the owner is a container. Don't kill the proxy process. Stop the container instead.

Free the port or pick another one

You have two clean options. Stop the old container (docker stop web1), or move the new one to a free host port such as -p 8081:80. In the lab, docker stop web1 released 8080 at once. ss showed no listener and a new container took 8080 without errors. You don't need docker rm to free a port.

One trap waits on the retry. The failed run still created web2, and docker ps -a listed it as Created. Running again with the same name, even on a new port, failed:

docker: Error response from daemon: Conflict. The container name "/web2" is already in use by container "dfb7802a...". You have to remove (or rename) that container to be able to reuse that name.

Run docker rm web2 first. After that, docker run -d --name web2 -p 8081:80 nginx:1.30.6-alpine started, and both http://127.0.0.1:8080/ and http://127.0.0.1:8081/ returned 200.

Fix bind: address already in use

When no container owns the port

For this case the lab started a plain host process on port 8082 with python3 -m http.server 8082. Then it asked Docker for the same port:

docker: Error response from daemon: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint web3 (3f7ab854...): Error starting userland proxy: listen tcp4 0.0.0.0:8082: bind: address already in use.

docker ps --filter publish=8082 printed nothing. Docker's own table was clean, so the daemon tried to open the socket and the kernel said no. That is the difference between the two messages. "Already allocated" comes from Docker's records. "Address already in use" comes from the operating system.

Find the process with ss and stop it

Ask the kernel who is listening:

sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :8082'

LISTEN 0      5            0.0.0.0:8082      0.0.0.0:*    users:(("python3",pid=752469,fd=5))

Run it with sudo. In the lab, plain ss without root listed the docker-proxy socket on 8080 with an empty process column. This tip comes from a highly voted answer by Jamie on the Postgres port question: "If lsof -i :5432 doesn't show you any output, you can use sudo ss -lptn 'sport = :5432' to see what process is bound to the port."

After kill 752469, the listener was gone. The failed container already existed, so docker start web3 was enough, and port 8082 returned 200. On a real server, the owner is usually a packaged service: nginx or apache2 on 80 and 443, postgresql on 5432, mysql on 3306. Stop and disable it with sudo systemctl disable --now nginx, or move your container to another host port. If a database on the host is the reason you can't connect at all, the PostgreSQL Docker auth guide and the MySQL Docker access denied guide cover the login errors that follow.

Fix port conflicts in Docker Compose

Another Compose project holds the port

Compose names projects after their folder. Two folders with the same service and the same ports: line collide:

services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.30.6-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8090:80"

docker compose up -d in projA started. The same command in projB failed with Bind for 0.0.0.0:8090 failed: port is already allocated. Running docker compose down in projB would not help, because projB doesn't own the port.

Compose writes the project name and its folder into container labels. Ask for them:

docker ps --filter publish=8090 \
  --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Label \"com.docker.compose.project\"}}\t{{.Label \"com.docker.compose.project.working_dir\"}}"

The output named proja and its full path. docker compose ls listed the same project with its compose file. docker compose -p proja down removed it from any directory, and projB then started and served 200 on 8090.

The restart: unless-stopped line matters here. A container with a restart policy comes back with the Docker daemon. In the 29.9.2 lab, a container started with --restart unless-stopped was up again on its port right after dockerd restarted, so an old stack you forgot about can hold a port after every reboot. Take it down with docker compose down, not just docker stop. A UI like Portainer also shows each stack and its published ports in one place.

Scaling a service with a fixed host port

docker compose up -d --scale web=2 on the same file started web-1 and then failed on web-2 with Bind for 0.0.0.0:8090 failed: port is already allocated. Every replica asks for the same host port. Give Compose a range instead:

services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.30.6-alpine
    ports:
      - "8091-8092:80"

With the range, both replicas started. docker compose ps showed one on 8091 and one on 8092. If you put a reverse proxy in front, you can drop the host port entirely and let the proxy reach the containers over the Compose network. The Traefik labels guide and the Nginx Proxy Manager guide both work that way.

Bind to one IP or let Docker pick a port

Same port on different host IPs

A host port is only taken on the address it is bound to. In the lab, -p 127.0.0.1:8095:80 and -p 127.0.0.2:8095:80 ran side by side, and both addresses returned 200. A third container with plain -p 8095:80 then failed with listen tcp4 0.0.0.0:8095: bind: address already in use. Note that this case produces the kernel message, not the Docker one, even though only containers were involved.

Binding to 127.0.0.1 is a good habit anyway. The Docker port publishing docs warn: "Publishing container ports is insecure by default. Meaning, when you publish a container's ports it becomes available not only to the Docker host, but to the outside world as well."

Let Docker choose a free host port

Publish only the container port and Docker picks a free host port:

docker run -d --name rnd -p 80 nginx:1.30.6-alpine
docker port rnd

80/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:32768
80/tcp -> [::]:32768

The Compose file reference says the same about ports:. You can give both sides "or just the container port. In the latter case, the container runtime automatically allocates any unassigned port of the host" (Compose services reference). This suits test stacks and CI runs where nobody types the URL by hand.

Newer Docker error wording

Docker Engine 29 messages

The same two tests inside docker:29.9.2-dind produced longer messages with a new prefix:

docker: Error response from daemon: failed to set up container networking: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint web2 (e1f0829e...): Bind for :::8080 failed: port is already allocated

docker: Error response from daemon: failed to set up container networking: driver failed programming external connectivity on endpoint web3 (d9beba20...): failed to bind host port 0.0.0.0:8082/tcp: address already in use

Search for the tail of the line, not the prefix. Bind for :::8080 is the IPv6 side of the same conflict, and failed to bind host port ... address already in use replaces the older Error starting userland proxy text. The causes and fixes are the same as above. docker ps --filter publish=8080 worked unchanged on 29.9.2, and netstat -ltnp inside the dind host still showed docker-proxy as the listener.

If you hit permission errors before you even get to the port problem, fix access to the daemon first with the docker.sock permission guide. The Uptime Kuma guide shows this same port error for a second copy of an app on 3001.

FAQ

What does "port is already allocated" mean in Docker?

Another container already publishes that host port. Docker checks its own records and refuses the mapping. Run docker ps --filter publish=PORT to see which one, as in SO 46176584.

How do I find which process is using a port on Linux?

Run sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :PORT'. The users: column shows the process name and PID. If it says docker-proxy, a container owns the port. See SO 38249434.

Why does docker ps show nothing but the port is still in use?

A process outside Docker holds the port, such as a host nginx, apache2 or postgresql service, or another container bound to a specific host IP. In the lab, docker ps --filter publish=8082 was empty while ss showed python3. Threads like SO 37971961 end with stopping the host service.

Can two Docker containers use the same port?

Yes on the container side, and on the host side if they use different host IPs. Both test containers listened on 80 inside. On the host, 127.0.0.1:8095 and 127.0.0.2:8095 worked together, but a third on 0.0.0.0:8095 failed.

Does stopping a container free its port?

Yes. After docker stop web1, ss showed nothing on 8080 and a new container took it. A restart policy can bring the old one back with the daemon, so use docker compose down or docker rm for stacks you no longer want.

How do I let Docker pick a free port automatically?

Publish only the container port, for example -p 80 or ports: ["80"], then read the result with docker port NAME. The lab got 32768. The Compose ports reference documents the same behavior.

Another container already publishes that host port. Docker checks its own records and refuses the mapping. Run docker ps --filter publish=PORT to see which one, as in SO 46176584.

Run sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :PORT'. The users: column shows the process name and PID. If it says docker-proxy, a container owns the port. See SO 38249434.

A process outside Docker holds the port, such as a host nginx, apache2 or postgresql service, or another container bound to a specific host IP. In the lab, docker ps --filter publish=8082 was empty while ss showed python3. Threads like SO 37971961 end with stopping the host service.

Yes. After docker stop web1, ss showed nothing on 8080 and a new container took it. A restart policy can bring the old one back with the daemon, so use docker compose down or docker rm for stacks you no longer want.

Publish only the container port, for example -p 80 or ports: ["80"], then read the result with docker port NAME. The lab got 32768. The Compose ports reference documents the same behavior.

Meta title: CI/CD Pipeline Design Improvement Roadmap

Meta description: Follow a practical CI/CD pipeline design improvement roadmap to identify bottlenecks, optimize workflows, strengthen security, and improve delivery performance.

A CI/CD pipeline improvement roadmap helps engineering teams make software delivery faster, more reliable, and more secure without adding unnecessary complexity. The most effective approach is to measure the current pipeline, identify the biggest bottlenecks, prioritize changes by impact, and validate each improvement against delivery performance and cost.

The goal is not simply to reduce pipeline runtime. A pipeline that finishes faster but misses tests, produces inconsistent builds, or makes deployments riskier is not an improvement.

Research supports this broader view. Google’s 2025 DORA report drew on more than 100 hours of qualitative research and survey responses from nearly 5,000 technology professionals. Its findings emphasized that AI amplifies existing organizational strengths and weaknesses, while increased AI adoption remained associated with delivery-stability challenges. For CI/CD teams, the practical lesson is clear: automation and speed deliver more value when supported by strong testing, reliable workflows, and effective controls. research

This guide outlines a practical CI/CD pipeline design improvement roadmap, including assessment steps, optimization priorities, examples, and metrics teams can use to measure progress.

1. What Is a CI/CD Pipeline Improvement Roadmap?

A CI/CD pipeline improvement roadmap is a prioritized plan for evaluating and improving the automated processes used to build, test, secure, package, and deploy software.

Continuous integration (CI) automates activities such as building code and testing changes as developers integrate them.

Continuous delivery (CD) keeps validated software ready for release, typically with controlled production deployment.

Continuous deployment takes the process further by automatically releasing qualifying changes to production.

A roadmap connects these activities to measurable outcomes: shorter feedback loops, fewer avoidable failures, more predictable releases, improved security, and controlled infrastructure costs.

The right sequence depends on the team’s current maturity. A team struggling with flaky tests should address test reliability before investing heavily in parallel execution. A team with stable tests but long runner queues may benefit more from capacity planning and job scheduling.

2. CI/CD Pipeline Design Improvement Roadmap: Six Steps

2.1 Establish a baseline before changing the pipeline

Start by examining recent pipeline runs rather than relying on one unusually fast or slow execution.

Collect data on:

  • Median and 90th-percentile pipeline duration.
  • Time spent waiting for runners versus executing jobs.
  • Build, test, and deployment failure rates.
  • Frequency of reruns without code changes.
  • Infrastructure and CI/CD platform costs.
  • Time from code commit to a usable test result or production release.

GitLab’s pipeline-efficiency documentation identifies job duration, stage dependencies, runner capacity, dependency installation, image size, and flaky tests as factors that can affect performance.

Practical output: A baseline report identifying the three biggest sources of delay or instability.

For example, a 25-minute pipeline might spend 12 minutes installing dependencies, eight minutes running tests sequentially, and five minutes waiting for runners. Each problem requires a different intervention, so the breakdown matters more than the total alone.

2.2 Map the pipeline and identify its critical path

Document the path from a code change to a successful release. Include triggers, jobs, dependencies, artifacts, security checks, approval gates, deployment environments, and rollback procedures.

A typical workflow looks like this:

  1. Code commit or pull request
  2. Linting, static checks, and build
  3. Automated tests and security scans
  4. Package and publish versioned artifact
  5. Deploy to staging and verify
  6. Production release, monitoring, and rollback readiness

This is an illustrative workflow; the exact stages and approval requirements depend on the application and its risk.

Look for jobs that block other jobs unnecessarily, expensive work repeated across stages, and checks that report failures too late. GitLab supports dependency-based scheduling with needs, allowing eligible jobs to start when their actual dependencies finish rather than waiting for an entire stage.

The key question is: Which step determines the earliest point at which the pipeline can deliver a trustworthy result? Improve that critical path first.

2.3 Prioritize high-impact CI/CD pipeline optimization

Once the bottlenecks are understood, choose targeted changes. Avoid redesigning the entire pipeline at once.

Problem Improvement Important safeguard
Repeated dependency downloads Cache dependencies and reusable build inputs Validate cache keys and treat restored content carefully
Long sequential test stages Run independent tests in parallel Confirm that resource contention does not erase the benefit
Slow job startup Use appropriately sized runners and lean build images Monitor cost and queue time
Feedback arrives too late Run fast, high-signal checks earlier Retain required test coverage
Flaky tests cause reruns Investigate test isolation, timing, and dependencies Track quarantined tests and set a plan to restore them
Unnecessary jobs run on every change Use path-based rules or conditional execution Verify that shared-code changes still trigger relevant checks
Build output differs between environments Build once and promote the same versioned artifact Preserve provenance and verify artifact integrity

GitHub’s documentation distinguishes caching reusable dependencies from storing workflow artifacts. It also warns that caches are not inherently verified and should never contain secrets.

The improvement principle is simple: remove repeated work, shorten unnecessary waits, and make failures easier to diagnose without weakening controls.

2.4 Build security and release reliability into the design

Security should be part of the pipeline rather than a final check performed just before release.

The NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) recommends integrating secure development practices into the software development lifecycle. Its guidance covers protecting software from unauthorized changes, producing secure releases, and responding to vulnerabilities.

Prioritize these controls:

  • Access control: Give pipeline jobs only the permissions they need.
  • Secret management: Store credentials in a dedicated secret-management system, not in source code, logs, or dependency caches.
  • Dependency security: Scan third-party packages and container images for known vulnerabilities.
  • Artifact integrity: Record the source revision and build details associated with each release artifact.
  • Deployment protection: Require appropriate approvals or additional checks for high-risk production changes.
  • Recovery: Maintain tested rollback or roll-forward procedures and monitor application health after deployment.

For GitHub Actions, the official security guidance recommends minimizing token permissions and pinning third-party actions to full commit SHAs to reduce supply-chain risk.

Not every project needs the same security gates. A documentation change and a production database migration have different risk profiles. Apply controls according to the potential impact of failure, while retaining mandatory checks for all relevant changes.

2.5 Standardize repeatable workflows

As teams improve individual pipelines, they often accumulate duplicated configuration, inconsistent deployment steps, and one-off scripts that are difficult to maintain.

Standardization helps address this problem.

Create reusable pipeline templates for common workflows, such as:

  • Building and testing a service.
  • Packaging and scanning a container image.
  • Deploying to staging.
  • Promoting an approved artifact to production.
  • Performing post-deployment verification.

Keep project-specific logic configurable rather than copying entire pipeline definitions between repositories. Version shared templates, test changes before broad adoption, and document how teams can override defaults safely.

A useful design rule is to build an artifact once and promote that same artifact through environments. Rebuilding separately for staging and production can introduce differences between what was tested and what was released.

This is also where platform engineering can help: teams can offer a supported deployment path with secure defaults while preserving flexibility for unusual workloads.

2.6 Measure results and repeat the improvement cycle

A CI/CD pipeline improvement roadmap should include a review process, not just a list of engineering tasks.

DORA’s current software delivery performance model uses five metrics, grouped into throughput and instability. These help teams assess delivery outcomes rather than judging pipeline quality by runtime alone.

Metric What it tells you
Change lead time How long a change takes to move from version control to production
Deployment frequency How often the application is deployed
Failed deployment recovery time How quickly the team recovers from a failed deployment
Change fail rate How often deployments require immediate intervention
Deployment rework rate How much deployment activity is unplanned work resulting from production incidents

Pair these outcome metrics with pipeline-level measurements, including queue time, execution time, flaky-test rate, rerun frequency, and cost per pipeline run.

Avoid setting speed targets in isolation. A shorter pipeline is useful only if it preserves meaningful validation and improves the developer experience. Compare similar workloads over time, and measure performance at the application or service level rather than assuming that every team should have identical targets.

3. A Practical 30–60–90-Day Improvement Plan

The following schedule is an illustrative starting point, not an industry benchmark. Adjust it to the size, risk, and complexity of your systems.

3.1 Days 1–30: Assess and establish visibility

  • Baseline pipeline duration, failures, queue times, and costs.
  • Map critical dependencies and release controls.
  • Fix the most disruptive flaky tests or recurring infrastructure failures.

Deliverable: Baseline dashboard and prioritized backlog.

3.2 Days 31–60: Optimize and remove measurable bottlenecks

  • Improve caching and dependency installation.
  • Parallelize independent jobs where resources allow.
  • Move fast, reliable checks earlier.
  • Strengthen permissions, secret handling, and artifact management.

Deliverable: Tested improvements with before-and-after results.

3.3 Days 61–90: Standardize and make improvements sustainable

  • Introduce reusable templates for common workflows.
  • Add release health checks and recovery drills.
  • Review delivery metrics, infrastructure spending, and developer feedback.
  • Assign owners and schedule regular pipeline reviews.

Deliverable: Documented standards and a recurring improvement process.

4. CI/CD Pipeline Design Examples

These examples illustrate how the roadmap can be applied to different bottlenecks. The results are hypothetical, not measured case studies.

Scenario Initial problem Improvement strategy Success measure
Web application Dependency installation dominates runtime Cache dependencies, use lean build images, and validate cache behavior Lower median runtime and fewer setup delays
Microservices platform Many jobs wait for unrelated stages Define explicit dependencies and parallelize independent tests Shorter critical path without higher failure rates
Financial application Manual release steps and inconsistent approvals Automate repeatable checks, restrict production permissions, and document approvals Fewer manual errors and more auditable releases
Data-intensive service Database changes make deployments risky Add migration validation, compatibility checks, backup verification, and recovery testing Fewer migration-related incidents and faster recovery

The right solution depends on the root cause. Adding more runners will not fix flaky tests, and parallelizing every job may increase cost without meaningfully improving the critical path.

For teams reviewing their broader engineering setup, resources from Heloix may provide additional context on technology and business needs. Any pipeline-specific implementation should still be evaluated against the team’s architecture, security requirements, and measured bottlenecks.

5. Frequently Asked Questions

5.1 What is the first step in improving a CI/CD pipeline?

Measure the current pipeline and identify its main bottleneck. Collect representative data on job duration, queue time, failure patterns, and cost before choosing an optimization.

5.2 How can teams make CI/CD pipelines faster?

Start by removing repeated work, caching suitable dependencies, running independent jobs in parallel, reducing unnecessary setup, and reporting failures earlier. Validate that these changes preserve test coverage and deployment reliability.

5.3 Which metrics should teams track?

Use pipeline-level metrics such as duration, queue time, failure rate, and reruns alongside DORA’s five software delivery performance metrics. Together, these show whether faster automation is improving actual delivery outcomes.

5.4 How often should a CI/CD pipeline be reviewed?

Review pipeline health regularly, such as during a monthly engineering review, and after significant incidents or architectural changes. High-change or high-risk systems may need more frequent reviews. The important part is to compare results against a baseline and assign ownership for follow-up.

5.5 Should every project use the same CI/CD pipeline?

No. Teams can standardize common workflows and security defaults, but pipelines should reflect differences in application architecture, testing needs, deployment risk, and compliance obligations.

6. Conclusion

A successful CI/CD pipeline design improvement roadmap is an ongoing engineering practice, not a one-time configuration exercise. Establish a baseline, identify the critical path, remove unnecessary work, strengthen security and release controls, and measure the effect of each change.

The most valuable improvement is not necessarily the one that saves the most seconds. It is the one that helps the team deliver useful changes with less waiting, fewer avoidable failures, and greater confidence in every release.

title: 5 Reasons Your AWS Bill Keeps Growing (Even When Nobody Uses Your App)
summary:
You built a small side project on AWS. Traffic is basically zero. Yet every month the bill creeps up, and the line items look like error codes: USE1-NatGateway-Hours, USE1-PublicIPv4:InUseAddress...

If that sounds familiar, you're not bad at AWS. Most surprise bills come from the same five causes, and each one takes only a few minutes to check.

Note: Prices below are AWS list prices for US East (N. Virginia), checked in November 2026. Other regions can cost more, and AWS updates prices over time. Always confirm on the official pricing pages (links at the end).

  1. Resources that charge just for existing

Many AWS services bill by the hour, not by how much you use them. If the resource exists, the meter is running.

The classic example is the NAT Gateway:

$0.045 per hour, which is about $32.85 a month, even with zero traffic
Plus $0.045 per GB of data it processes

Lots of beginner tutorials create a NAT Gateway so private subnets can reach the internet. The tutorial ends, the gateway stays.

Other usual suspects:

Public IPv4 addresses. Since February 1, 2024, every public IPv4 address costs $0.005 per hour (about $3.60 a month), whether it's attached to something or not.
EBS volumes from instances you stopped or terminated. The disk can outlive the server.
Load balancers with no traffic.
RDS databases left running 24/7 for a test you finished weeks ago.

Quick check: find unattached EBS volumes and unused Elastic IPs in your current region:

bash
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available \
--query "Volumes[].[VolumeId,Size]" --output text

aws ec2 describe-addresses \
--query "Addresses[?AssociationId==null].[PublicIp,AllocationId]" --output text

If anything shows up that you don't need, delete it. Stopping isn't always enough.

  1. Resources hiding in another region

The AWS console only shows resources in the region you currently have selected.

So if a tutorial had you build in N. Virginia (us-east-1) but you normally work in Oregon (us-west-2), those first resources seem to vanish. They haven't. They're still running, and still billing.

Quick check (console): open Resource Groups & Tag Editor → Tag Editor, set Regions to All regions and Resource types to All supported resource types, then search. Anything you don't recognize deserves a closer look.

Quick check (CLI): list EC2 instances in every region:

bash
for r in $(aws ec2 describe-regions --query "Regions[].RegionName" --output text); do
echo "== $r"
aws ec2 describe-instances --region "$r" \
--query "Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name]" --output text
done

  1. Data transfer and logs that add up quietly

Data transfer out: sending data from AWS to the internet costs money. You get 100 GB per month free, but that allowance is shared across all regions combined, not per region. Serving images or video straight from an EC2 instance can burn through it quickly.

CloudWatch Logs: ingesting logs costs $0.50 per GB, plus about $0.03 per GB per month to store them. Two things make this sneaky:

Verbose debug logging you turned on "just for today" and never turned off.
Log groups keep data forever by default.

title: Best Amazon SES Alternatives in 2026
summary:
Amazon SES is built for sending at scale from inside AWS, and many teams start there. The best Amazon SES alternatives are for when you want more around the send: no sandbox approval, a dashboard with logs, templates you can edit without a deploy, delivery events without wiring up Amazon SNS, and marketing email in the same place. This guide compares ten Amazon SES (AWS SES) alternatives on price, free tier, SMTP, webhooks, deliverability and campaigns, using each vendor's own pricing and product pages, checked between October 27 and November 8, 2026.

We make Cresca, so it is listed first. Every other entry is described from the vendor's own public pages, without ranking claims about them. Prices and plans change, so confirm on each vendor's site before you switch.

What is Amazon SES?

Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES, often called AWS SES) is the email sending service inside Amazon Web Services. You send through its API or SMTP interface, pay per email, and build the rest yourself: event handling through other AWS services, templates, a log your support team can read, and any campaign tooling. That trade is what makes SES cheap per email, and it is why teams look for an Amazon SES alternative once they want those parts ready-made.

Why teams look for an Amazon SES alternative

  • The sandbox. AWS places all new accounts in the SES sandbox, where you can only send to verified addresses and domains, up to 200 messages per 24 hours and 1 per second. Leaving it means requesting production access; AWS says its support team gives an initial response within 96 hours.
  • Plumbing for events. Deliveries, bounces, complaints, opens and clicks are published as events to Amazon SNS, EventBridge, CloudWatch or Data Firehose, which you configure and consume yourself.
  • Pricing plans. New SES accounts start on the Essentials plan at $0.16 per 1,000 emails; Pro and Enterprise plans add fixed monthly charges per account and region. The full breakdown is below.
  • No campaign tools. SES sends marketing email, but its pages describe no campaign builder, so newsletters need another tool on top.
  • Amazon Pinpoint's end of support on October 30, 2026 left teams that used Pinpoint for email campaigns looking for a new home for contacts, templates and campaigns.

Amazon SES pricing: what you actually pay

Amazon SES pricing is per email, with extras for attachments, dedicated IPs and deliverability tools. Figures from the Amazon SES pricing page, checked on November 8, 2026, for the first 10 million emails a month:

Pro plan $0.22 $105 per account per region
Enterprise plan $0.23 $500 per account per region
  • Which rate applies: AWS says accounts with no metered SES activity since June 1, 2025 start on the Essentials plan from July 21, 2026.
  • Attachments: $0.12 per GB of attachment data sent.
  • Dedicated IPs: $24.95 per IP per month (standard), or managed dedicated IPs at $15 per account per month plus $0.08 per 1,000 emails.
  • Virtual Deliverability Manager: $0.07 per 1,000 emails for SES deliverability insights.
  • Free tier: new AWS customers get up to $200 in AWS Free Tier credits that can be used on SES.

At 10,000 emails a month, that is about $1.00 à la carte or $1.60 on Essentials, and $26.60 if you add one standard dedicated IP. The per-email price is rarely the reason teams switch. The cost is the work around it: the sandbox request, wiring delivery events through Amazon SNS or EventBridge, a template workflow, and a place where support can see what happened to an email.

How we compared these Amazon SES alternatives

Each service is described from its own pricing pages and documentation, not from third-party reviews. We looked at:

  • Setup: whether you can send to real recipients on day one, or wait for an approval step like the SES sandbox.
  • Price: the free option and the cheapest paid plan, in US dollars per month.

  • Sending: REST API, SMTP relay, SDKs and webhooks on all plans.
  • Marketing: Separate marketing plans priced by contacts.

  • Free option: A developer plan with 100 emails per month.

  • Sending: Email API, SMTP, event webhooks and inbound processing.
  • Marketing: Broadcast message streams in the same account.

  • Sending: API and SMTP, with event webhooks on paid plans.
  • Marketing: Marketing Campaigns, purchased as a separate plan.

5. Mailgun

Mailgun calls itself a transactional email delivery service and API for developers.

  • Free option: 100 emails per day.
  • Paid: Basic starts at $15/month for 10,000 emails.
  • Sending: RESTful APIs and SMTP relay, with webhooks.
  • Marketing: Not stated on its pricing page.

MailerSend presents itself as a team-friendly email API for apps, with SMS and WhatsApp alongside email.

  • Free option: 500 emails per month.
  • Paid: Hobby is $7/month for 5,000 emails.
  • Sending: Email API, SMTP relay and webhooks.
  • Marketing: No separate marketing product described; bulk emailing on paid plans.

7. Mailtrap

Mailtrap offers email sending for developer and product teams, with email marketing and a testing sandbox as separate products.

  • Free option: 4,000 emails per month, up to 150 per day.
  • Paid: Basic is $15/month for 10,000 emails.
  • Sending: API, SMTP relay and webhooks.
  • Marketing: Email Marketing, sold separately.

8. Mailchimp Transactional (formerly Mandrill)

Mailchimp Transactional is sold as an add-on to a Mailchimp plan.

  • Free option: Up to 500 free emails to a verified domain for new users.
  • Paid: $20 per block of 25,000 emails, plus a Mailchimp Standard or Premium plan.
  • Sending: API, SMTP integration and webhooks.
  • Marketing: Through the Mailchimp plan it is added to.

9. Brevo

Brevo sells email marketing, automation and transactional email in one account, alongside SMS and other channels.

  • Free option: A free plan, with no credit card needed.
  • Paid: Starter is $9/month from 5,000 emails a month.
  • Sending: SMTP relay and API keys for transactional email, with transactional webhooks.
  • Marketing: Campaigns, templates and segmentation on the same plans; automation from the Standard plan.

10. SMTP2GO

SMTP2GO describes itself as an email and SMS delivery service that you connect through SMTP or its API.

  • Free option: Up to 1,000 emails a month.
  • Paid: Starter is $10/month for 10,000 emails, with extra emails at $1 per thousand.
  • Sending: SMTP relay and HTTP API, with webhooks and reporting.
  • Marketing: Not stated on its pricing page.

Deliverability: what changes when you leave Amazon SES

Switching providers does not reset your domain's reputation, but it does change who signs and sends your mail. Plan for these:

  • Authentication records. Add the new provider's DKIM records and, where it uses a custom MAIL FROM domain, its SPF record. Keep your DMARC record; a domain can only have one.
  • Shared or dedicated IPs. Most plans in this list send from shared IPs. A dedicated IP needs steady volume and a warm-up period before it helps.
  • Bounces and complaints. Carry your SES suppression list over, so addresses that bounced or complained are not mailed again from the new provider.
  • Gradual moves. Switch one email type at a time and watch bounce and complaint rates before moving the next.

In Cresca, domain setup shows the DKIM and SPF records to publish and checks whether your domain has a DMARC record. Hard bounces, repeated soft bounces, complaints and unsubscribes are suppressed automatically, for API email and campaigns alike. See the email deliverability guide for the full checklist.

  1. Verify your sending domain in Cresca by publishing the DNS records it shows, and keep SES sending while you switch. See the quickstart.
  2. Create a sending-access API key and store it as CRESCA_API_KEY.
  3. Move templates. Paste your SES template HTML into Cresca's template editor with Import HTML, mark variables with triple braces and publish.
  4. Swap the send call, one email type at a time, starting with a low-risk one such as a welcome email.
  5. Keep a list of addresses that bounced or complained on SES and leave them out of your Cresca sends, so your new domain setup starts with a clean reputation.
  6. Switch the rest once the dashboard timeline looks right, then retire the SES configuration.

Hi Ana, your account is ready.

    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY}`,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'Idempotency-Key': 'welcome/user-123',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: 'Acme ',
    to: 'ana@example.com',
    subject: 'Welcome to Acme',
    html: '
Hi Ana, your account is ready.
',

const body = await res.json();

Frequently asked questions

What is the best Amazon SES alternative?

It depends on what you need around sending. If you also send newsletters and campaigns, Cresca puts a transactional email API and AI-designed marketing email on one plan, with no sandbox and a dashboard for every email. Resend, Postmark, SendGrid, Mailgun, MailerSend, Mailtrap, Mailchimp Transactional and SMTP2GO focus on sending, and Brevo combines marketing with transactional email.

Is there a cheaper alternative to Amazon SES?

Per email, rarely. Amazon SES costs $0.10 per 1,000 emails à la carte or $0.16 on the Essentials plan, which is less per email than the paid plans in this list. Alternatives charge more per email but include the dashboard, logs, templates, delivery events and support that you would otherwise build or buy around SES. Several also have free plans, from 1,000 emails a month on SMTP2GO to 4,000 on Mailtrap.

How long does it take to get out of the Amazon SES sandbox?

You request production access from the SES console or the AWS CLI, giving your use case and website. AWS says its support team provides an initial response within 96 hours. Until then you can only send to verified addresses, up to 200 messages per 24 hours.

Is Amazon SES affected by the Amazon Pinpoint end of support?

No. Amazon Pinpoint's engagement features ended on October 30, 2026, but Amazon SES continues. Teams that used Pinpoint for email campaigns, segments and journeys need another place for them, which is what the Pinpoint migration guide covers.

Can I keep my domain authentication when I leave SES?

You keep your domain, but each provider signs mail with its own DKIM keys, so you add the new provider's DNS records. DKIM records for different providers can sit side by side, which lets you move one email type at a time and keep SES running until the switch is complete.

Do SES alternatives support SMTP?

Most of the services in this comparison offer an SMTP relay as well as an HTTP API. Cresca sends through its HTTP API today, and an SMTP relay is on its roadmap.

title: Shadow AI apps: what IT can do about tools staff build with AI
summary:
Last updated 25 October 2026. Written by TeamOnly. We make one of the places builders can deploy to, and we say so where it comes up.

Quick answer: Assume these apps already exist. Find them without blame, then give builders one approved place to deploy: behind your company login, with a named owner for every app. A one-page policy covers the rest.

Banning AI tools rarely works. It moves the apps somewhere you can't see. This page covers what shadow AI is, the real risks of AI-built internal apps, how to find what already exists, and a policy you can copy.

What is shadow AI?

Three terms that get mixed up. They describe the same habit at different stages.

  • Shadow IT: software and services people use for work without IT knowing or approving. A personal file-sharing account, a project tool paid on someone's card.
  • Shadow AI: the same, with AI tools. Staff paste company data into chat assistants or AI features that IT has not reviewed.
  • Shadow AI apps: the newer part. Staff use Claude Code, Cursor, Lovable, Replit, Bolt or v0 to build a working app, publish it, and send the link to coworkers. The app holds company data and keeps running.

The third one is different because it lasts. A chat is over in a minute. An app has users, data and a link that keeps working, often on the builder's own account.

Vendor research: In a Retool survey of 307 CTOs, CIOs and CISOs in May 2026, 8% said they had strong governance of AI-built internal tools, and 5% were very confident they could see everything running. Security company Red Access reported finding more than 380,000 publicly reachable assets on the main vibe-coding platforms. About 5,000 looked like company tools, and more than 2,000 of those held sensitive business, operational or personal data.

Checked 25 October 2026. Sources: Retool AI Governance Report 2026 (a vendor survey, June 2026), summary of Red Access's research on The Hacker News (a contributed article, May 2026).

What can go wrong with AI-built internal apps?

The code is rarely the main problem. Where the app lives, and who can open it, usually is.

  • Public links with company data. Many app builders publish to the open web unless you pay for, or find, the private option. A link nobody was told about still gets shared, and sometimes indexed by search engines.
  • Shared passwords. A password on the whole app ends up in chat threads and emails. The app can't tell who did what, and people who leave still know it.
  • Apps on personal accounts. The app runs on whatever platform the builder signed up for, billed to their card, under their login. The company has no admin access to it and may not know it exists.
  • No owner when someone leaves. When the builder leaves, the app either keeps running with nobody responsible for it, or stops when their card is cancelled. Either way, the team that relied on it finds out last.
  • No list of what exists. You can't review, fix or retire an app you don't know about. Without a list, every one of these risks is invisible.
  • Secrets in code, databases left open. AI tools sometimes write API keys into code that runs in the browser, where anyone who opens the app can read them. A hosted database with row-level security turned off can be read without going through the app at all.

How do I find the apps that already exist?

No single tool finds them all. These steps, together, find most of them in an afternoon.

  1. Ask, without blame. Send one short message: "If you built a tool with AI that coworkers use, tell us. Nothing gets switched off, we want to help you keep it running safely." Builders are usually glad someone asked.
  2. Check expense reports and card statements. Look for Lovable, Replit, Bolt, Vercel, Netlify, Supabase, Cursor and Claude subscriptions. A builder platform on an expense report usually means an app somewhere.
  3. Check what people signed in to with their work account. Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra both list the third-party apps people connected with their work account, and sign-in logs show which ones they use. Builder platforms show up there when people sign up with "Sign in with Google" or Microsoft.
  4. Look for app addresses. Search DNS or web proxy logs, and your company chat, for addresses like *.lovable.app, *.replit.app, *.vercel.app, *.netlify.app and *.pages.dev. Links in chat are often the fastest way to find the apps people actually use.
  5. Check browser and device inventories, if you have them. If you manage browsers or laptops, the inventory shows AI extensions and apps like Cursor or Claude installed. That tells you who is building, not what they built, so follow up by asking.
  6. Write it down. One row per app: name, owner, where it is hosted, what data it holds, who uses it. That sheet is your first inventory, and it tells you which apps to move first.

A vibe coding policy you can adopt

Short enough that people read it. Change the parts in [brackets] and send it.

Policy: tools built with AI
