   Cursor, Lovable, Replit, Bolt, v0 or similar) that someone other than its
   builder uses.
2. Building is allowed. Anyone may build tools for their own work. You don't
   need permission to try an idea.
3. Where apps live. Apps that coworkers use are deployed to [our approved
   host]. Not on a personal account, and not on public hosting.
4. Login comes first. Every app asks for a company account before it shows
   any screen or data. No shared passwords and no public links.
5. Data. Internal work data is fine. Customer personal data, payment card
   data, health data and passwords to other systems need a check with IT
   first. Company data never goes into an app on a personal account.
6. Keys and passwords. API keys and passwords go in the host's secret
   settings. Never in the code, and never in chat.
7. Every app has an owner. The owner keeps it working and decides who can
   open it: the whole company or a named list of people.
8. When someone leaves. Before someone leaves or changes role, their apps are
   handed to a new owner. An app nobody takes over is turned off.
9. Report, without blame. If you find an app with company data that anyone
   can open, tell [IT contact]. Nobody gets in trouble for reporting.
10. Review. IT reviews the list of apps every [quarter]. Apps nobody has used
    in [90 days] may be deleted after asking the owner.

People build these tools because they solve real problems. A ban doesn't remove the problem, it moves the tool to a personal account. One approved place to deploy gets you the same tools, behind your login, in a list you can read.

  • Sign out everywhere. An admin can sign a builder out of every terminal and the dashboard at once.

Questions people ask

Shadow AI apps go one step further: the staff member is not just using a tool, they built one, and it holds company data.

A ban rarely removes the need. People build these tools because they solve real problems, so a ban moves them to personal accounts where you can't see them. Most companies do better with a short policy and one approved place to deploy.

Ask, without blame. Then check expense reports for Lovable, Replit, Vercel and similar subscriptions, the list of third-party apps people connected with their work account in Google Workspace or Microsoft Entra, and DNS or chat logs for addresses like *.lovable.app or *.vercel.app.

What should a vibe coding policy include?

What people may build, where apps must be deployed, that every app needs a company login, what data is allowed, where keys and passwords go, who owns each app, and what happens when the owner leaves. The policy on this page fits on one page and can be copied as is.

Are AI-built apps a security risk?

For internal tools, the bigger risk is usually where the app lives, not the code: a public link, a shared password, a personal account, keys written into the code, or nobody responsible once the builder leaves. Each of those can be fixed by the place the app is deployed to.

title: TCP Provider: The Wait Operation Timed Out - It Was the Firewall, Not SQL Server
summary:
We moved this site's database to a new SQL Server, and the first time I tried to connect from my own PC, sqlcmd sat for a few seconds and then printed this:

Sqlcmd: Error: Microsoft ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server : TCP Provider: The wait operation timed out.
Sqlcmd: Error: Microsoft ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server : Login timeout expired.
Sqlcmd: Error: Microsoft ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server : A network-related or instance-specific error
has occurred while establishing a connection to SQL Server. Server is not found or not accessible.

The connection string was right, the password was right and the server was running - the website was using it at that very moment. The problem was one layer below SQL Server: the new host's firewall was silently dropping connections from my IP address. The next day the same error came back, because my home internet connection had been given a new IP. Here is how to tell which layer is failing, and how to fix each one.

The short version: "TCP Provider: The wait operation timed out" (SQL Server error 258) means your computer sent a connection request and never got an answer. Something in the network path - usually a firewall - is dropping it. Run Test-NetConnection -Port 1433. If TcpTestSucceeded is False, fix the firewall (the server's, the host's or the cloud provider's) before touching SQL Server settings.

What the error actually means

A timeout is different from a refusal. When a port is closed but the machine is reachable, the server answers straight away with "no" and you get an error quickly, such as No connection could be made because the target machine actively refused it (error 10061). A timeout means there was no answer at all. Your packets went out and nothing came back, which is exactly what a firewall does when it drops traffic instead of rejecting it. The Login timeout expired line is just the client giving up after waiting. And error 258 is the Windows code for a wait that timed out, which is why it appears in SQL Server Management Studio and .NET versions of the same failure.

So the error tells you something useful: SQL Server probably never saw your attempt. Changing the password, the database name or the SQL login will not help.

Step 1: test the port, not SQL Server

PowerShell has a built-in test that tries a plain TCP connection to a port:

# Can this machine open a TCP connection to the SQL Server port at all?
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 203.0.113.10 -Port 1433

# The line that matters:
# TcpTestSucceeded : False   -> blocked or nothing reachable; SQL Server never saw the attempt
# TcpTestSucceeded : True    -> the network path is open; look at SQL Server itself

This takes SQL Server, drivers, logins and connection strings out of the picture. When I ran it against both servers from the same PC, the answer was immediate:

PS> (Test-NetConnection 203.0.113.10 -Port 1433).TcpTestSucceeded   # new server
False
PS> (Test-NetConnection 198.51.100.20 -Port 1433).TcpTestSucceeded  # old server, same PC
True

Same computer, same network, same moment: one server reachable and one not. That rules out my PC, my router and my ISP blocking 1433, and points straight at the new server's side. (On macOS or Linux, nc -vz 203.0.113.10 1433 does the same job.)

Step 2: what to check when TcpTestSucceeded is False

Work from the outside in. Each of these drops traffic silently, which is what produces the timeout:

  1. The hosting or cloud firewall. Shared hosting panels, VPS providers and cloud platforms (Azure network security groups, AWS security groups) usually block 1433 from the internet by default and let you allow specific IP addresses. This was my case: the host only accepted SQL connections from listed addresses, and mine was not on the list. Once it was added, TcpTestSucceeded turned True and sqlcmd connected first time.
  2. Windows Firewall on the SQL Server machine. Even with the host's firewall open, Windows Defender Firewall on the server needs an inbound rule for TCP 1433.
  3. A different port. Named instances such as SQLEXPRESS use a dynamic port by default, not 1433. If the instance is not set to a fixed port, testing 1433 will fail even though SQL Server is fine. Check the port in SQL Server Configuration Manager, or connect with server\instance and let the SQL Server Browser service (UDP 1434) tell the client the port.
  4. TCP/IP disabled. SQL Server Express installs with TCP/IP turned off. In SQL Server Configuration Manager, enable it under SQL Server Network Configuration, set the port under IP Addresses → IPAll, and restart the SQL Server service. Strictly, this one usually gives a refusal rather than a timeout, but it is on every "allow remote connections" checklist for a reason.

For the Windows Firewall rule, allow your address rather than the whole internet:

# On the SQL Server machine (elevated PowerShell): allow 1433 only from your address
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "SQL Server 1433 from office" `
  -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 1433 `
  -RemoteAddress 203.0.113.45 -Action Allow

Step 3: when it worked yesterday - your IP changed

The day after everything worked, the same timeout came back. Nothing had changed on the server. Running Test-NetConnection again gave False, and checking my public IP explained it:

# Your public IP - the address the server's firewall sees, not your 192.168.x.x LAN address
(Invoke-RestMethod https://api.ipify.org)

Home and many office broadband connections get a dynamic IP from the ISP, which changes after a router restart or simply every few days. An allow-list with a single address breaks the moment it does. The options, from quickest to most robust:

  • Update the allowed address each time it changes - fine if it is rare.
  • Allow a small range from your ISP if the host supports CIDR ranges. This trades some security for fewer surprises; keep the range as tight as you can.
  • Use a static IP from your ISP, or a VPN with a fixed exit address, and allow only that.
  • Do not expose SQL Server at all: connect through an SSH tunnel or a VPN into the server's network, or run your scripts on the server itself. This is what I would recommend for anything beyond a small site.

Whatever you choose, do not solve this by opening 1433 to everyone. A SQL Server listening on the public internet gets password-guessing attempts within hours.

Step 4: when TcpTestSucceeded is True but it still fails

If the port test passes, the network is fine and the error will usually be different:

Error What it means
Login failed for user (18456) You reached SQL Server; the login, password or authentication mode is wrong
Cannot open database requested by the login Login is fine; the database name is wrong or the user has no access to it
The certificate chain was issued by an authority that is not trusted Encryption is on by default in newer drivers; install a trusted certificate or set TrustServerCertificate=true for testing
Still "wait operation timed out", only on large queries A query or command timeout rather than a connection timeout; look at the query, not the network

Two connection-string details are worth checking while you are there: put the port after a comma (Server=host,1433), not a colon, and give slow networks a longer connect timeout:

Server=203.0.113.10,1433;Database=MyDb;User Id=app_user;Password=;
TrustServerCertificate=true;Connect Timeout=30;

If you work with sqlcmd a lot, two other errors that cost me time on the same database are 'Scripting variable not defined' and Msg 1934 about QUOTED_IDENTIFIER. And if the connection works locally but the deployed app gets a 500 instead, see ASP.NET Core on Plesk: every error I hit.

FAQ

What does 'TCP Provider: The wait operation timed out' mean?

Your computer sent a connection request to SQL Server and got no answer at all. Something in the network path, usually a firewall, dropped it. SQL Server most likely never saw the attempt, so changing the password or database name will not help.

What is SQL Server error 258?

Error 258 is the Windows code for a wait that timed out. In SQL Server connection errors it appears with 'The wait operation timed out' and means the client gave up waiting for a reply from the server.

How do I test if SQL Server port 1433 is open?

In PowerShell run Test-NetConnection -Port 1433 and look at TcpTestSucceeded. True means the network path is open; False means a firewall or routing problem, or SQL Server is not listening on that port. On macOS or Linux use nc -vz 1433.

Why did my SQL Server connection stop working when nothing changed?

If the server only accepts connections from allowed IP addresses, your public IP may have changed. Home and many office connections get a dynamic IP from the ISP. Check your current public IP and update the allow-list, or use a static IP, a VPN or an SSH tunnel.

How do I allow remote connections to SQL Server Express?

Enable TCP/IP in SQL Server Configuration Manager, set a fixed port under IPAll (usually 1433), restart the SQL Server service, add a Windows Firewall inbound rule for that port, and allow your IP in any hosting or cloud firewall in front of the server.

Is it safe to open port 1433 to the internet?

No. A SQL Server reachable from anywhere attracts automated password-guessing quickly. Allow only the IP addresses that need access, or reach the server through a VPN or SSH tunnel instead.

What is the difference between a connection timeout and a refused connection?

A refused connection gets an immediate answer: the machine is reachable but nothing is listening on the port. A timeout gets no answer at all, which usually means a firewall is silently dropping the traffic. The fix for each is in a different place.

title: Claude Code moved its Explore subagent off Haiku in 2.1.198. Two env vars get it back for 60% less.
summary:
In February a post here said Claude Code's built-in Explore subagent is hard-coded to Haiku. I measured something different last week: on 2.1.318, an Opus session's Explore calls all ran on Opus.

Both were right. I ran 205 headless sessions across 26 Claude Code versions to find out when it changed.

  • Up to 2.1.197: Explore ran on Haiku in every run.
  • From 2.1.198: Explore runs on whatever model your main session uses.
  • Cost on Opus: a delegated code search went from $0.18 to $0.37 per run (+105%).
  • The fix: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=haiku plus CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1. Explore went back to Haiku in 36 of 36 runs, cost dropped 60%, and it found the same answers.

The setup

Each run asks Claude Code a "find every place" question in an open-source repo (undici, fastify, cachetools, Python-Markdown, anyio, zod) and tells it to use the Explore subagent. Headless claude -p, read-only tools, stream-json logs. The subagent's model comes from its own messages and the per-model cost split in the log.

  • Version history: 18 versions from 2.1.0 to 2.1.318, then a bisection over the npm releases in between. Main model fixed to Opus 4.5, because the API refuses Opus 5.5 below 2.1.280.
  • Settings test: 2.1.318 with Opus 5.5 on 12 questions × 3 runs, under three settings.

Pre-registered on GitHub before the runs, with two dated amendments (one is my own bisection bug, explained below).

The settings

Setting Explore ran on Found Cost/run
Default Opus 5.5 100% $0.38
CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=claude-haiku-5-5 Opus 5.5 99% $0.37
CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=haiku + CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 Haiku 5.5 100% $0.15

Setting the subagent model alone did nothing for Explore. That matches the sub-agents docs: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL is only a default, and the FORCE flag (2.1.257+) is what applies it to every subagent. The docs also mention a project subagent named Explore with model: haiku. I didn't test that route.

To use it, put both in your shell or in settings.json:

{ "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "haiku", "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE": "1" } }

Note that FORCE applies to every subagent, not only Explore.

A mistake I made on the way

My first bisection said the switch was at 2.1.176. The script checked for Haiku with a regex that could never match the log format, so every probe looked like "not Haiku". When I read the raw logs, 2.1.176 through 2.1.186 were all Haiku. I fixed the check, re-ran the bisection and logged it as an amendment. The wrong-step probes are in the data too.

Limits

Two questions per version in the history, so it shows which model ran, not how good it was. One machine, one account, one prompt. Defaults can change again.

Data

All 205 runs (model, cost split, recall, every answer) are public under CC BY 4.0:

  • Data page: https://tokensave.app/data/claude-subagent-model-by-version
  • GitHub (pre-registration, scripts): https://github.com/johnisking/token-cost-by-language/tree/main/claude-subagent-model-by-version

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: Same Prompt, Two JSON Shapes, and a Validator That Passed Both
summary:
Six hundred markdown files landed in an inbox folder, and my only job was to turn them into a one-page morning report. The plan looked trivial: send each file to a model, get back four fields, append a line of JSONL, render a table. I gave myself forty-eight hours to make that loop boring, so like an idiot I built the happy path first.

The happy path held for about six hours. The full run exited 0, the report rendered, and nobody on the receiving end noticed that one column had quietly stopped meaning anything. These are the field notes: what I tried, where it broke, and the small harness I would keep for next time.

The constraints I actually had

Before the timeline makes sense, here is the shape of the problem.

  1. Roughly 600 small text files per night, growing by maybe 5% a week.
  2. Four output fields per file: category, severity, needs_human, summary.
  3. A morning report that a human reads, so a wrong column is worse than a missing row.
  4. No budget, which meant a free tier and a free machine, and no assumption of either staying stable.

That last one is the constraint people skip, and it produced every bug below. If your model access can change shape between Tuesday and Wednesday, then your real interface is not the API — it is the contract you wrote down and test.

Hour 0–6: the validator that agreed with everything

I wrote the extraction call, a parser, and a validator, and all three passed on the first twenty files. The validator was a dataclass with type annotations checked by isinstance, which felt rigorous and was mostly theater.

# validate_v0.py -- the version that lied to me
FIELDS = {"category": str, "severity": str, "needs_human": bool, "summary": str}


def validate_v0(payload: dict) -> list[str]:
    errors = []
    for key, expected in FIELDS.items():
        if key not in payload:
            errors.append(f"missing {key}")

title: Your Free Server Is Not Your Laptop: A Parity Probe for Five Assumptions That Break on Deploy
summary:
You push. The build goes green. Then it 502s.

Sound familiar? The gap is almost never your business logic. It is the environment you quietly assumed.

So here is a myth-busting FAQ about free tiers. Claims developers repeat. Evidence you can collect yourself. A corrected mental model after each one.

Two claims are on the table, and only two. MonkeyCode offers free model access, and it has a free server option. Those are operator-supplied availability claims.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Everything else — quotas, hardware, sleep policy, storage lifetime — stays unmeasured until you probe it. I have not run the code below against that server for this article. You are the one collecting numbers.

Why "works on my machine" is a measurement problem

Your laptop and any remote host are different computers. That is not a bug. It is a fact you forgot to write down.

When something breaks on deploy, you are not debugging code. You are debugging unstated assumptions. So stop guessing and start enumerating.

Myth 1: "Same app, same environment"

The claim: I run the same build, so behavior must match.

But env vars differ. Working directories differ. The process supervisor differs. Even the timezone and locale may differ quietly.

A 12-factor app reads config from the environment. That does not mean both environments hold the same config.

Corrected model: a deployment is a new environment, not a copy of yours. Enumerate the facts you depend on, then assert them at boot.

  • Which env vars are present? Presence matters more than value.
  • What is process.cwd()? Relative paths resolve against it.
  • Is the directory writable? Many apps assume yes.

Myth 2: "If it binds locally, it's reachable"

The claim: the port works on my machine, so the host will expose it.

Locally you often bind 127.0.0.1. That is loopback only. A container or VM needs 0.0.0.0 to accept outside traffic.

Also many platforms inject PORT. Hardcoding 3000 is a guess dressed as a default.

Corrected model: binding is a two-part contract — address and port. Read both from the environment. Verify from outside, not inside.

Myth 3: "A restart is a no-op"

The claim: restarting just reruns my process, so nothing changes.

But in-memory state vanishes. Counters reset. Any local file cache might vanish too, depending on where you wrote it.

Write to /tmp? Maybe ephemeral. Write to cwd? Maybe not writable at all.

Corrected model: assume nothing survives a restart. Then prove which parts do. Persistence is a measurement, not a vibe.

Myth 4: "Free model access means free inference capacity"

The claim: the endpoint answers, so throughput is a solved problem.

Access is not capacity. A reachable endpoint tells you one thing only: it answered once, from one place, at one moment.

So measure rather than assume. Latency from your laptop is not latency from the host. Rate behavior under concurrency is unknown until you push.

Corrected model: treat free access as an envelope you discover. Send a small burst, record outcomes, and set your own concurrency ceiling below it.

Myth 5: "Local latency predicts user latency"

The claim: my API call takes 300ms at home, so users see 300ms.

Your laptop sits close to your network. The host sits somewhere else, with its own route and its own queue.

Add cold start on top. The first request after idle is not the thousandth request in steady state.

Corrected model: latency is a property of a path, not of a function. Measure from where the code runs.

The artifact: a /probe endpoint and a restart test

Here is the smallest thing that converts assumptions into evidence. One file, zero dependencies, Node 18+.

import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { writeFileSync, mkdirSync, existsSync, readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const bootId = randomUUID();
const startedAt = Date.now();
const markerPath = join(tmpdir(), "probe-marker.json");
const target = process.env.PROBE_TARGET ?? "";

function writable(dir) {
  try {
    mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });
    writeFileSync(join(dir, `.probe-${bootId}`), "ok");
    return true;
  } catch { return false; }
}

function previousBoot() {
  if (!existsSync(markerPath)) return null;
  try { return JSON.parse(readFileSync(markerPath, "utf8")); } catch { return null; }
}

async function upstream() {
  if (!target) return { skipped: true };
  const t0 = performance.now();
  try {
    const r = await fetch(target, { method: "HEAD" });
    return { status: r.status, ms: Math.round(performance.now() - t0) };
  } catch (e) {
    return { error: String(e?.message ?? e), ms: Math.round(performance.now() - t0) };
  }
}

const server = createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.url !== "/probe") { res.writeHead(404).end("not found"); return; }
  const prev = previousBoot();
  writeFileSync(markerPath, JSON.stringify({ bootId, startedAt }));
  const body = {
    bootId,
    uptimeSec: Math.round((Date.now() - startedAt) / 1000),
    node: process.version,
    platform: process.platform,
    env: { PORT: process.env.PORT ?? null, NODE_ENV: process.env.NODE_ENV ?? null },
    files: {
      cwd: process.cwd(),
      cwdWritable: writable(process.cwd()),
      tmp: tmpdir(),
      tmpWritable: writable(tmpdir())
    },
    previousBoot: prev,
    upstream: await upstream()
  };
  res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" });
  res.end(JSON.stringify(body, null, 2));
});

server.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000), "0.0.0.0", () => {
  console.log(`probe on 0.0.0.0:${process.env.PORT ?? 3000}`);
});

Note the deliberate choices. It binds 0.0.0.0. It reports env var presence, never values. It returns no secrets.

Run the restart test

Now call it twice, with a restart in between.

curl -s https://YOUR_HOST/probe | tee probe-1.json
# restart the service however your host does it
curl -s https://YOUR_HOST/probe | tee probe-2.json
diff <(jq -S . probe-1.json) <(jq -S . probe-2.json)

Then read the diff like a diagnostic.

  • bootId changed? Good, the process really restarted.
  • previousBoot is null? That marker did not survive. Your /tmp is not durable.
  • cwdWritable is false? Drop file-based caches from that path.
  • upstream.ms is large or errors? Measure from the host, not your desk.

Set PROBE_TARGET to your model endpoint URL to include it. A HEAD may return 405; that is still a useful reachability signal.

A probe that leaks paths is a reconnaissance gift. Gate it behind a header or remove it after the test.

Never reuse /probe as your production health check. It writes files. Health checks should not.

Why "works on my machine" is a measurement problem

Your laptop and any remote host are different computers. That is not a bug. It is a fact you forgot to write down.

When something breaks on deploy, you are not debugging code. You are debugging unstated assumptions. So stop guessing and start enumerating.

Myth 1: "Same app, same environment"

The claim: I run the same build, so behavior must match.

But env vars differ. Working directories differ. The process supervisor differs. Even the timezone and locale may differ quietly.

A 12-factor app reads config from the environment. That does not mean both environments hold the same config.

Corrected model: a deployment is a new environment, not a copy of yours. Enumerate the facts you depend on, then assert them at boot.

  • Which env vars are present? Presence matters more than value.
  • What is process.cwd()? Relative paths resolve against it.
  • Is the directory writable? Many apps assume yes.

Myth 2: "If it binds locally, it's reachable"

The claim: the port works on my machine, so the host will expose it.

Locally you often bind 127.0.0.1. That is loopback only. A container or VM needs 0.0.0.0 to accept outside traffic.

Also many platforms inject PORT. Hardcoding 3000 is a guess dressed as a default.

Corrected model: binding is a two-part contract — address and port. Read both from the environment. Verify from outside, not inside.

Myth 3: "A restart is a no-op"

The claim: restarting just reruns my process, so nothing changes.

But in-memory state vanishes. Counters reset. Any local file cache might vanish too, depending on where you wrote it.

Write to /tmp? Maybe ephemeral. Write to cwd? Maybe not writable at all.

Corrected model: assume nothing survives a restart. Then prove which parts do. Persistence is a measurement, not a vibe.

Myth 4: "Free model access means free inference capacity"

The claim: the endpoint answers, so throughput is a solved problem.

Access is not capacity. A reachable endpoint tells you one thing only: it answered once, from one place, at one moment.

So measure rather than assume. Latency from your laptop is not latency from the host. Rate behavior under concurrency is unknown until you push.

Corrected model: treat free access as an envelope you discover. Send a small burst, record outcomes, and set your own concurrency ceiling below it.

Myth 5: "Local latency predicts user latency"

The claim: my API call takes 300ms at home, so users see 300ms.

Your laptop sits close to your network. The host sits somewhere else, with its own route and its own queue.

Add cold start on top. The first request after idle is not the thousandth request in steady state.

Corrected model: latency is a property of a path, not of a function. Measure from where the code runs.
